chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad from al-Khashshab from Ibn Baqqah from Mu'adh ibn Thabit from 'Amr ibn Jumay' from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said:

Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'O Ali! This Religion is robust, so delve into it with gentleness, and do not make the worship of your Lord hateful to yourself. For the excessive one (meaning the one who goes to extremes), there remains no back (to ride upon) nor land (to travel through). Therefore, act like the one who hopes to die in old age, and beware with the caution of the one who fears dying tomorrow.'

key_terms.الْمُفْرِطَ: The one who goes to extremes/excessive
key_terms.الْمُنْبَتَّ: The uprooted plant (metaphor for the excessive one)
key_terms.فَأَوْغِلْ فِيهِ بِرِفْقٍ: Delve deeply into it with gentleness/moderation

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic principle of moderation in worship according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This foundational hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of *wasatiyyah* (moderation) in worship, warning against *al-mubalaghah* (exaggeration) that causes believers to tire of their duties. The metaphor of the 'uprooted plant' (*al-munbat*) illustrates how excessive rigor leads to spiritual burnout, while the advice to act as one expects to die of old age encourages consistent, enduring practice rather than sporadic intensity. This teaching is central to Shia jurisprudence for balancing ritual devotion with worldly responsibilities, ensuring faith remains sustainable throughout a believer's life.
